query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled trace amount of vanadium into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will enable the formation of a stable, self-lubricating microstructural phase across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, resulting in lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its standard heterogeneous microstructure and existing friction and wear characteristics.
generation.intervention: Microalloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with a controlled addition (e.g., 0.5–1 atomic %) of vanadium.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribological tests performed under progressively increasing temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C, under variable loads and in ambient (oxidizing) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The vanadium addition is expected to induce a phase change that leads to a more homogeneous microstructure and/or the in situ formation of a lubricious vanadium-rich phase or oxide at the contact interface.
generation.mechanism: Vanadium acts to modify the microstructural evolution during high-temperature sliding by promoting the formation of a stable lubricious phase (such as a vanadium oxide) that dissipates shear stress and inhibits dislocation-driven damage. This phase could also serve as a barrier against wear by reducing direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby maintaining low friction and wear rates even as operational conditions vary.
generation.predicted_outcome: The vanadium-doped CoCrFeNi alloy will show a significantly reduced coefficient of friction and lower wear rates over the full temperature range (RT to 800 °C) when compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi alloy without vanadium addition, which suffers performance limitations in tribological behavior across the wide temperature range.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only under conditions where the temperature remains between room temperature and 800 °C, under moderate to high loads, and in oxidizing or ambient environments that promote controlled oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact nature of the lubricious phase (e.g., whether a vanadium-rich oxide forms) in the CoCrFeNi matrix and how scalable and stable the effect is across the entire temperature range without additional alloying or processing modifications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one set of CoCrFeNi alloy doped with 0.5–1 atomic % vanadium. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled and varying loads in ambient (oxidizing) environments. Post-test, perform microstructural characterizations using microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) and surface analysis (e.g., XPS) to determine any formation of vanadium-induced phases.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear rates under specified loads and temperatures
Microstructural phase analysis pre- and post-sliding (e.g., phase homogeneity, presence of lubricious vanadium-rich phase/oxide)
Surface chemical state and composition via XPS or related techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-doped CoCrFeNi alloy does not consistently exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline across the full temperature range, or if the anticipated stable lubricious phase (e.g., vanadium-rich oxide) is not observed in the microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloys are of interest to many researchers due to the possibility of shaping their functional properties by, among other things, the use of alloying additives. One approach to improving the wear resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi alloy is modification through the addition of titanium. However, in this study, an alternative solution was explored by adding vanadium, which has a completely different effect on the material’s structure compared to titanium. The effect of vanadium additives on changes in the microstructure, hardness, and wear resistance of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy. The base alloys Al0.7CoCrFeNi and Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 were obtained by induction melting. The results showed that the presence of vanadium changes the microstructure of the material. In the case of the base alloy, the structure is biphasic with a visible segregation of alloying elements between phases. In contrast, the Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 alloy has a homogeneous solid solution bcc structure. The presence of vanadium increased hardness by 33%, while it significantly reduced friction wear by 73%. ## Abstract
AbstractHigh Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have garnered attention due to their remarkable tribological attributes. Predominantly, failure mechanisms in HEAs emanate from stress‐induced dislocations, culminating in crack propagation and film delamination. In this study, we report on the synthesis of 2D HEA of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 which facilitates shear‐induced energy dissipation at sliding interfaces. The ball‐on‐disk tribological investigations demonstrate unprecedentedly low average coefficients of friction (0.076) and wear rates (10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1) under high contact pressures (0.936 GPa) within ambient conditions. Employing multi‐scale characterizations alongside molecular dynamic simulations, we elucidate that the presence of the HEA triggers tribocatalytic activity under high contact pressures emerging as a pivotal factor in extending lubricant lifespan during tribological tests. The resilient lubriciousness coupled with the facile spray coating methodology of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 in ambient environments paves the way for the development of a new class of solid lubricants based on 2D HEA.
